## Standard

<a id="Captures"></a>

### Captures

`Captures` · `src/syntax.ts:133`

The names a language's queries give to what they catch, each with what the reader does with it: the contract between a language node and the reader. A capture whose name is not here is ignored (tree-sitter's convention: those that start with _ only serve a predicate).

Source: Trame, the contract between the language nodes and the syntax reader; local.definition follows tree-sitter's locals convention · `https://tree-sitter.github.io/tree-sitter/4-code-navigation.html`

| Constant | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `literalText` | `literal.text` | A text written as a value. Its value is its parts, escape sequences decoded |
| `literalNumber` | `literal.number` | A number, its minus sign included: -1 is one literal |
| `literalRegex` | `literal.regex` | A regular expression |
| `literalTemplate` | `literal.template` | A text with substitutions; without any, it is a text. What it substitutes is read on its own |
| `literalKey` | `literal.key` | A key that is not an identifier: a value written where a name goes. No name capture removes it |
| `literalPart` | `literal.part` | A fixed part of a text or a template, as written |
| `literalEscape` | `literal.escape` | An escape sequence of a text or a template, decoded as the language's escapes say |
| `literalSubstitution` | `literal.substitution` | What a template substitutes: shown as an ellipsis, read as code |
| `name` | `name` | Written like a value but names something (an identifier key, a module, a type): no literal, import or global inside it counts |
| `importValue` | `import.value` | A module imported as a value. It wins over import.type for the same module |
| `importType` | `import.type` | A module imported: for its types only, unless import.value names it too |
| `importComputed` | `import.computed` | An import whose path is computed: no reading can tell what it loads |
| `localDefinition` | `local.definition` | A name the body defines (tree-sitter's locals convention). It hides a global of the same name |
| `global` | `global` | What may reach outside the body: an identifier, a member, a construction |
| `globalName` | `global.name` | In the match of a global, the name a local definition would hide (Date, in Date.now) |
| `entry` | `entry` | What the body gives: its default export |
| `declaration` | `declaration` | A declaration of a module: an inline body is looked for in the one on its line |
| `body` | `body` | In a declaration, the value of a property: the body, when the property is the body's field |
| `bodyName` | `body.name` | In the match of a body, the name of its property |
| `rolePrefix` | `role.` | Opens the name of a role capture: role.index catches the place of an index. What follows is a role of LiteralRoles |
| `callee` | `callee` | In the match of a role.argument, the name of the function called |
| `parameter` | `parameter` | A parameter the body declares itself (a Terraform variable): the graph must pass it, and only it |
| `output` | `output` | What the body gives back by name (a Terraform output) |

## Decisions

<a id="LiteralCategories"></a>

### Categories of literals

`LiteralCategories` · `src/syntax.ts:223`

How the catalogue sorts the literals it lists: the first category whose rule a literal meets is its own. A hint to sort the catalogue, not a truth about the value. A rule may name the kinds of literal it takes, patterns its text must all match (a number's text is its value), and a pattern of the line it appears on.

| Category | Value |
|---|---|
| regular expression | { kinds: regex } |
| HTTP status | { kinds: number, text: { source: ^[1-5]\d\d$ }, near: { source: writeHead\|status\|code, flags: i } } |
| number | { kinds: number } |
| colour | { text: { source: #[0-9a-fA-F]{3,8}\b\|rgba?\( } } |
| media type | { text: { source: ^[a-z]+\/[a-z0-9.+-]+(;\|$), flags: i } } |
| address | { text: { source: ^https?:\/\/ } } |
| file | { text: { source: \.(json\|md\|ts\|tf\|lock\|html\|css\|db)$\|^\.{0,2}\/ } } |
| markup | { text: { source: <[a-z]+[\s>], flags: i } } |
| separator | { text: { source: ^[\s\p{P}\p{S}]*$, flags: u } } |
| sentence | { text: { source: \p{L}[\s\p{L}'\u2019,]*\s+\p{L}, flags: u }, { source: [a-z\u00e0-\u00ff], flags: i } } |
| identifier | { text: { source: ^[\p{L}\d_.:-]+$, flags: u } } |
| template | { kinds: template } |
| text | {  } |

## Architecture decisions

<a id="PredicatesAsTreeSitterReadsThem"></a>

### tree-sitter says what it keeps aside

`PredicatesAsTreeSitterReadsThem` · `src/syntax.ts:308` · status: **held**

The predicates of a query that tree-sitter does not evaluate are those tree-sitter itself keeps aside when it compiles the query: no pattern of Trame's looks for them.

Context: The kind of a language looked for the predicates of its queries with a pattern of its own (a number sign, a name, a question or an exclamation mark): it said again what the grammar of queries says, a text inside a query could fool it, and it was a literal of the language.

Consequences: The port SyntaxTrees gives, for a query, the predicates tree-sitter keeps aside when it compiles it; the reader gives them by query; the kind of a language makes each one an error. The constants of TreeSitterQueries say which predicates tree-sitter evaluates; the standard names its highlighting, "scheme", until a package gives the grammar of queries, which would let Trame read them as a language.

| Rejected | Why |
|---|---|
| A syntax element for a predicate | it would say how a predicate is written, and still need a pattern to find one in a query |
| A pattern among the standard's constants | it would count as one more predicate tree-sitter evaluates |
| The queries as a language now | no maintained package gives their grammar in WebAssembly |

- Decided by: trame
- Serves: [A specification that runs](product.md#ExecutableSpecification)
- Applied by: [Syntax reader](#SyntaxReader), [Syntax trees](architecture.md#SyntaxTrees)

<a id="ReadLanguagesAlike"></a>

### Every language is read alike, with tree-sitter

`ReadLanguagesAlike` · `src/syntax.ts:291` · status: **held**

A language is a node of the graph: its grammar, its queries, the escapes of its texts, examples of what must be found. One reader reads every body with it, and knows the captures of the queries, not the node types of any grammar.

Context: Trame reads bodies to check them and to find their literals, in every language a product's bodies are written in: TypeScript and Terraform today.

Consequences: The checks of a body are the same for every language; the queries of a language are checked against what tree-sitter evaluates, and its examples are played at every build; the port SyntaxTrees is the only place that touches tree-sitter, and no tree crosses it.

| Rejected | Why |
|---|---|
| The TypeScript compiler API | it reads one language, and each other one would need a reader of its own |
| Regular expressions | the old Terraform driver: blind to texts, comments and nesting |

- Decided by: trame
- Serves: [A specification that runs](product.md#ExecutableSpecification)
- Applied by: [Syntax reader](#SyntaxReader), [Checks of a body](#BodyChecks), [Syntax trees](architecture.md#SyntaxTrees)

## Functions

<a id="BodyChecks"></a>

### Checks of a body

`BodyChecks` · `src/syntax.ts:279` · status: **held**

What a body may touch, read on its reading, the same for every language: the prelude's public API only as a value import; no other module of the project (a hidden dependency: declare it as a parameter); the platform (a package, a built-in module, a computed load, a global that reaches outside) only for the kinds that may touch it. A file body exports what it gives; a body follows the grammar of its language. A refused body is never run.

<a id="SyntaxReader"></a>

### Syntax reader

`SyntaxReader` · `src/syntax.ts:261` · status: **held**

Reads a body with the grammar and the queries of its language: the literals, the imports, what may reach outside, whether it gives something, and where it does not follow the grammar. It parses each file once in the process, again only when its text changed; an inline body is read in the property of its declaration. It knows the captures, and nothing of any grammar.

## Message catalog

<a id="LiteralRoles"></a>

### Roles of a literal

`LiteralRoles` · `src/syntax.ts:170`

What a literal does, from its place in the code, and how the catalogue says it. A language catches each place with a capture named role.<role>. The role of a literal is the smallest role capture that holds it; between two of the same size, the first role here. A literal that no role capture holds is "other".

<details><summary>The messages, in code</summary>

```typescript
() => ({
    /** The position in a list or a text. */
    index: () => "index",
    /** A text joined to another with + (before arithmetic: a text added is joined). */
    concatenation: () => "concatenation",
    /** An operand of + - * / % **, or of += and -=. */
    arithmetic: () => "arithmetic",
    /** An operand of & | ^ << >> >>>. */
    bitwise: () => "bitwise arithmetic",
    /** An operand of a comparison: === !== == != < <= > >=. */
    comparison: () => "comparison",
    /** What ?? and || fall back on, a parameter's default value. */
    default: () => "default value",
    /** An operand of &&, the condition of a choice. */
    condition: () => "condition",
    /** The value assigned with =. */
    assignment: () => "assignment",
    /** One of the two branches of a choice (a ? b : c). */
    branch: () => "branch of a condition",
    /** An argument of a call, or of a construction (new). */
    argument: (callee?: string) => (callee === undefined ? "argument" : `argument of ${callee}`),
    /** The value a variable starts with. */
    initial: () => "initial value",
    /** The value of a property of an object. */
    property: () => "property value",
    /** What a function returns. */
    returned: () => "returned value",
    /** An element of a list. */
    element: () => "element of a list",
    /** A case of a switch. */
    case: () => "case of a switch",
    /** A substitution of a template. */
    template: () => "in a template",
    /** A statement on its own, or a spread element. */
    statement: () => "statement",
    /** The value of an attribute of a markup element. */
    attribute: () => "attribute value",
    /** The content of a markup element: its text. */
    content: () => "content of an element",
    /** Any other place. */
    other: () => "other",
  }) satisfies Record<string, RoleLabel>
```
